replying_to: Replying to Parameterizing Activation Functions for Adversarial Robustness
display_title: Official Review of Paper3451 by Reviewer qjye

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a new activation function called Parametric Shifted Sigmoidal Linear Unit (or PSSiLU). This activation function requires 2 learnable parameters (as a single set of parameters is learned for the whole network). With this activation, the authors improve upon the state-of-the-art on CIFAR-10 against l-infinity perturbations of size 8/255 with a WRN-28-10 by achieving 61.96% robust accuracy.
content.main_review:
Pros:
* Thorough analysis of various parametric activation functions (to the best of my knowledge, this has not been done before).
* Improves upon SOTA on CIFAR-10 for identical model size (WRN-28-10) with 61.96% (vs 60.97% at the time of writing).

Cons:
* The activation only helps in the high-data regime (with the use of additional generated data). Without this extra regularization coming from the extra data, the proposed activation function hurts performance.
* Results vary a lot for different settings (CIFAR-100, ImageNette) and more often than enough the proposed activation does worse than PSiLU (proposed by Ramachandran et al., 2018).
* As such, one of the key claims in the abstract ("activation shapes with positive outputs on negative inputs") is not thoroughly validated in practice.

Specific comments:

1) Section 3 uses weak adversaries to determine which activation functions perform better. I'd rather see a strong adversary applied at smaller radii. While the Square and PGD results seem to correlate well on CIFAR-10, they do not correlate on ImageNette.

2) Is there an equivalent of Fig 4 for ImageNette?

3) While the jump from 54.07% to 58.21% when using PSSiLU instead of SiLU looks impressive, I'm questioning how the baseline networks were trained.  Sehwag et al. obtain 55.6% (on a ResNet-18 with ReLU) and Rebuffi et al. obtain 60.73% (on a WRN-28-10 with Swish/SiLU). These numbers are quite different from the 53.67% and 55.10% obtained in Table 2. Could the authors explain the difference in setup?

4) PSSiLU needs to be regularized so that $\beta$ remains small. That seems contradictory to the conclusion of Section 3 that "activation shapes with positive outputs on negative inputs". Similarly, PReLU which has infinite curvature is not more robust, which is contradictory to the high curvature hypothesis.

5) It would be good to see the full breakdown of AutoAttack (for the different attacks) for the best models. I don't expect any surprises, but since the authors have the AA logs to would be good to share them.

6) Axes labels are missing on almost all plots.

7) The paper uses image extracted from Tiny Images in the appendix and makes reference to it in the main text. This dataset should not be used (see https://groups.csail.mit.edu/vision/TinyImages/). Since it is not important to the message of the paper, I'd suggest removing it completely.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is well written. It contains a significant number of experiments. However, the synthesis of the results is quite simplistic and conclusions are drawn prematurely. In particular: (i) the proposed activation is not always beneficial; and (ii) it is unclear how parametric activations help robustness. For (ii), the authors claim that it allows the optimization to find a better minimum (but there is no comparison on the training set performance). In other words, it remains unclear how parametric activation functions improve robust generalization.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Thank you for the feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for the feedback.  Please find our responses below:
> The activation only helps in the high-data regime

We note that since we are using *synthetic data* from DDPM which is a generative model trained on the original dataset of interest.  Because of this there is no additional data collection or labelling cost incurred.  We also note that in many cases PSiLU and PSSiLU still outperform ReLU even without the use of additional data.   This is further confirmed by our model appearing in the RobustBench leaderboard under the category of “no extra data”. 

> Results vary a lot for different settings and more often than enough the proposed activation does worse than PSiLU (proposed by Ramachandran et al., 2018)

We emphasize that we are the first to explore the use of PAFs in conjunction with adversarial training, so investigating the impact of PSiLU and other preexisting PAFS in the adversarial setting is also a contribution of this paper.

> One of the key claims in the abstract ("activation shapes with positive outputs on negative inputs") is not thoroughly validated in practice.  Regularization of PSSiLU seems contradictory to the conclusion of Section 3 that "activation shapes with positive outputs on negative inputs". Similarly, PReLU which has infinite curvature is not more robust, which is contradictory to the high curvature hypothesis.

For clarification, the trends observed in Section 3 are used to motivate the design of PSSiLU rather than make conclusions about activation function shape and robustness.  Since in Section 3, we perform experiments on standard trained models against a weak adversary, we cannot make conclusions about robustness against strong adversaries.  We do include an analysis of learned activation shape of adversarially trained models in Section 4.3, where we observe that optimization tends towards the same properties observed on weak adversaries, but our only conclusion is that these qualities are correlated with better data fitting.

> Difference in numbers from Sehwag et al. and Rebuffi et al.
Our training pipeline is based off of Sehwag et al’s training pipeline, but there are differences in the additional data used by our model.  We use a publicly released DDPM dataset with 6M images (https://github.com/preetum/cifar5m) while Sehwag et al uses a DDPM dataset which they generated on their own with 15 million DDPM images.  Rebuffi et al. also uses a self-generated DDPM dataset, trains with TRADES, and uses additional techniques like weight averaging to improve performance.  The bulk of our experiments are using PGD adversarial training and we do not use weight averaging.

> TI-500k

We thank the reviewer for pointing out that TinyImages has been withdrawn.  We will remove the results corresponding to TI-500k from the Appendix.

> it is unclear how parametric activations help robustness. For (ii), the authors claim that it allows the optimization to find a better minimum (but there is no comparison on the training set performance). In other words, it remains unclear how parametric activation functions improve robust generalization.

Our conclusion is that PAFs help robustness by improving the model’s ability to fit the data (Section 4.3).  Comparison on training set performance is shown in Figure 5, where we plot the train PGD accuracy vs test PGD accuracy.  We find that PAFs can achieve high training accuracy, but have a larger generalization gap compared to non-PAFs.  This is why additional data and regularization helps improve the performance of PAFs.

> We also note that in many cases PSiLU and PSSiLU still outperform ReLU even without the use of additional data.

I apologize if my earlier comment was not formulated correctly. I meant that the parametric function proposed in the paper (PSSiLU) requires the additional regularization coming from this additional data (in this case synthetic). As such, it raises the question whether the function allows for too much freedom and will lead to overfitting in some regimes (ResNet-18, VGG-16 CIFAR-10 where the standard SiLU performs better; ImageNette). Another option is that PSSiLU induces some instability in training and results may have high variance. Did the authors do multiple training runs and would be able to provide standard deviation?

> We emphasize that we are the first to explore the use of PAFs in conjunction with adversarial training, so investigating the impact of PSiLU and other preexisting PAFS in the adversarial setting is also a contribution of this paper.

I fully agree (as noted in my original review). I would find an analysis of the different parametric activation functions very insightful. However, the paper falls slightly short on that point. The core analysis is performed against a weak adversary (which the authors agree is suboptimal: _"we cannot make conclusions about robustness against strong adversaries"_). I also fail to see how this analysis (against weak adversaries) motivates PSSiLU from a robustness standpoint: it seems to indicate that high curvature and positive values on
negative inputs could induce gradient obfuscation (or at least create loss landscapes that are harder to optimize). This observation is further confirmed by the need to regularize $\beta$. Maybe the authors could provide figure showing various loss landscapes?

> We use a publicly released DDPM dataset with 6M images (https://github.com/preetum/cifar5m).

Could the authors provide more details on how these images were labeled? The default labels seems to be generated by a classifier trained on ImageNet (or JFT): _"The unconditional images were then labeled by a 98.5% accurate Big-Transfer model"_. Side question: Is the model uploaded on RobustBench using these labels?

> The bulk of our experiments are using PGD adversarial training and we do not use weight averaging.

The results are still widely different from those obtained by Gowal et al. (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.03593.pdf) where ReLU obtains 50.80% and SiLU obtains >51% on a WRN-28-10 -- compared to 45.98% and 47.51%, respectively. Did the authors not use early stopping? If so, it might be valuable to understand why parametric activation function prevent robust overfitting.

> Comparison on training set performance is shown in Figure 5, where we plot the train PGD accuracy vs test PGD accuracy.

Apologies for missing Figure 5. Indeed parametric function seem to obtain a higher train robust accuracy (the caption or labels should specify that it is the robust accuracy that is measured and maybe also against which attack).

I am willing to increase my score if authors could provide:
* Provide standard deviations for some of their experiments
* Double-check that the analysis against weak adversaries is not flawed (e.g., by providing loss landscape and showing the behavior against a strong adversary at a lower perturbation radius for some of the activation considered)
* Provide clarification about the dataset used
* Explain further explain why baseline results are worse than the literature. If the explanation is due to early stopping, then a discussion on robust overfitting would be warranted.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a parametric activation function where we can control the shape of the activation function using two additional parameters, more specifically the first parameter alpha controls the curvature of the activation function and the second parameter beta controls the behaviour on negative inputs.  Firstly using a weak square attack on a standard trained model the authors empirically show the high influence on robustness on changing these parameters. Based on this hypothesis the authors propose an activation function PSSiLU which belongs to the SiLU class but consists of two additional parameters alpha and beta. Using this activation function instead of commonly used ReLU the authors show extensive gains in adversarial robustness on the CIFAR-10 dataset when using additional data from DDPM-6M. However, the gains are insignificant when not using any additional data. Overall the paper is well written, easy to follow and the experiments are well organized and clear.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

* The paper is well written and easy to understand. The experiments are properly thought off. For instance, variance is shown in figure-3 plots without which a clear understanding of the robustness is not possible. Similarly, the strong Auto-Attack is used for all the robust evaluations.
* The paper achieves good improvements in robustness on CIFAR10 with additional data (DDPM-6M) as compared to the existing art.
* Some of the limitations are also shown and addressed properly.

Weaknesses:

The major concerns are as follows:
* Though [1] has been referenced but I think a more detailed discussion on [1] is required in the paper. Some of the claims of both these papers are aligned. Both the works discuss how changing the curvature of activation functions can impact robustness. Though overall I think there are differences in both the papers but still novelty as compared to [1] needs to be discussed in detail.
* The results for SiLU reported in Table-2 seem to be suboptimal. These are lower than what is reported in figure-5 of [2]. In general, PReLU seems to degrade the results, is there any explanation for this?
* It's a little difficult to understand why at many places SiLU and PSiLU are better than PSSiLU. Though the former two are kind of a subset of PSSiLU. This makes me feel if the optimization on using the two additional parameters is quite tough? Can the authors share the results of PSSiLU on ResNet18 and WideResNet-28-10(if possible) for the CIFAR-10 dataset and the L-infinity threat model for 3-5 runs with different random restarts? This will certainly give a better understanding of the results. 
* It seems like more fine-tuning is required for the results reported where additional data is not used since these seem very suboptimal as compared to the existing methods. Could the authors clarify why they are low, figure-5 does not seem very convincing since even when using the additional data training accuracy is very high, thus overfitting is still present? Could the authors share their ResNet18 and WRN-28-10(if possible) with PSiLU and PSSiLU activations for AWP[3]? The authors can share for CIFAR10 with and without additional DDPM-6M dataset. This will help in understanding the approach better since AWP[3] is the current state of the art when extra data is not used and also helps in preventing overfitting. 
* The significant boost is reported only for the CIFAR10 dataset with additional data, while CIFAR100 or any other datasets have not been addressed properly. If possible could the authors show the results on using additional data for CIFAR-100 for WRN-28-10?

Some minor concerns are as follows:
* It seems like the results reported in table-8 are highly suboptimal. Since it is known that the results on using TI-500K additional data are generally better than on using DDPM-6M, however, these results show the opposite trend. Could the authors share the details on how the used TI-500K dataset for additional images?
* Generally it is well known that AWP[3] and TRADES are much better than PGD. Could the authors clarify why they have not used TRADES/AWP as their base method?
* In Figure-7 and Figure-6(c and d parts) could the authors clarify why the grey lines are not visible? Do all the grey lines coincide with a red line in these figures? Could the authors clarify what models and datasets they have used for the grey lines?
* It's quite surprising that for the main activation function proposed in the paper, PSSiLU the value of beta comes out to be zero at the end of training. Could the authors share a plot on how the values of alpha and beta of PSSiLU change during the course of training? If possible could the authors share the graph on how the values of alpha change during the course of training for PSiLU activation as well?
* Could the authors share the accuracy after each of the attacks present in AA attack that is APGD-CE, APGD-CE+DLR, APGD-CE+DLR+FAB and APGD-CE+DLR+FAB+Sqaure for the reported WRN-28-10 model on CIFAR-10 for ReLU, SiLU, PSiLU and PSSiLU activations.

I am willing to raise my score if the concerns are addressed properly.

[1] Singla, V., Singla, S., Jacobs, D., & Feizi, S. (2021). Low Curvature Activations Reduce Overfitting in Adversarial Training. ArXiv, abs/2102.07861.

[2] Gowal, S., Qin, C., Uesato, J., Mann, T.A., & Kohli, P. (2020). Uncovering the Limits of Adversarial Training against Norm-Bounded Adversarial Examples. ArXiv, abs/2010.03593.

[3] Wu, D., Wang, Y., & Xia, S. (2020). Revisiting Loss Landscape for Adversarial Robustness. ArXiv, abs/2004.05884.

Further, the novelty of the paper as compared to [1] needs to be properly addressed since both approaches have some similarities.

content.title: Thank you for the feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for the feedback.  We are still in the process of running experiments suggested by the reviewer (including AWP, CIFAR-100 with DDPM data, PSSiLU on multiple seeds), but we address additional clarification questions below:

> More detailed discussion on [1]

[1] explores the impact of curvature on robust overfitting and finds that low curvature tends to decrease the gap between train and test.  In our case we aren't concerned with overfitting; we are interested in robust accuracy.  We find that while the generalization gap is larger for PAFs (which optimize towards higher curvature), there is an increase in robust accuracy for smooth PAFs due to better data fitting during training.  Additionally, we experiment with learnable PAFs while [1] experiments with fixed activation functions.  We have incorporated a discussion of [1] in comparison to our work in Appendix B.

> The results for SiLU reported in Table-2 seem to be suboptimal. These are lower than what is reported in figure-5 of [2].

There are some differences in implementation between this work and [2] since the bulk of our experiments is based off Sehwag et al.’s training pipeline.  For instance, we don’t perform normalization on inputs and use a different learning rate scheduler.

> In general, PReLU seems to degrade the results, is there any explanation for this?

We believe this is related to findings from [1] where the authors define a notion of approximate curvature for non-smooth activations like leaky ReLU.  They find that as the parameter on Leaky ReLU (which corresponds to our parameter on PReLU) becomes negative the generalization gap increases.  In our results, we observe that the training robust accuracy for PReLU is not that much higher than ReLU, so having a larger generalization gap ends up harming robust accuracy for PReLU.

> Suboptimal results without additional data, overfitting with additional data

We believe that the suboptimal of PAFs in comparison to their nonparametric counterparts is due to overfitting.  PAFs can achieve very high training accuracy, but seem to have problems with generalization without the additional data to regularize.  While the training accuracy looks high in Figure 5 when additional data is present, the accuracy measured in the figure is only on the CIFAR-10 train set.  If we include measurements on additional data in addition to CIFAR-10, the accuracy is lower (about 75.8% for PSSiLU), so the model is not overfitting to the additional data.

> TI-500K procedure

We train with batches of 256 CIFAR-10 images and 256 TI-500K images.  We perform data augmentation (random crop, random horizontal flip) on CIFAR-10 images, but not on TI-500K images.  We do not normalize the data.

> Why PGD instead of TRADES and AWP

We base our training pipeline off of Sehwag et al’s training framework which incorporates PGD adversarial training, so we chose to use PGD adversarial training for the bulk of our experiments.  We provide experimental results for TRADES adversarial training in Appendix C.3.  We will also add results for AWP as suggested by the reviewer.

> Figure-7 and Figure-6 grey lines

The grey lines in this figure overlap with the red line.  Parameter values range between 5-8, the visual difference between these values is very small.  For these figures we take an aggregate over models trained with CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNette shown in the main body and appendix that use PGD adversarial training.

Sehwag, Vikash, et al. "Robust Learning Meets Generative Models: Can Proxy Distributions Improve Adversarial Robustness?" arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.09425 (2021).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors investigate the role activation functions play in the robustness of deep neural networks to adversarial attacks. Based on a parameter search, the authors claim that having a positive output for a negative input and a high curvature are useful for defending against adversarial attacks. The authors then design a parameterized activation function with two parameters that allow the networks to tune the aforementioned properties.

When testing their activation function on CIFAR-10 with and without adversarial attacks, the proposed activation functions sometimes performs slightly better when compared to existing activation functions such as ReLU and SiLU.
content.main_review:
STRENGTHS:

The authors investigate what aspects of activation functions are responsible for adversarial robustness. While there is existing work on this topic, the approach that the authors took regarding curvature is somewhat unique. There needs to be more investigation into the properties of activation functions and how they relate to adversarial robustness, in general.

WEAKNESSES:

While the experiments show having a positive output for a negative input and high curvature are correlated with better robustness, I do not think the authors have good evidence that this is the cause. While the authors mention work by [1], their results could possibly by explained by this work as they investigate how symmetry in activation functions is related to adversarial robustness. Though the activation functions that the authors use are not perfectly symmetric, allowing there to be a positive output for a negative input makes them closer to a symmetric function.

Work done in [2] investigates much of what the authors are doing in this paper. Though the authors do cite this paper, I do not think they mention the similarities. [2] uses learns a parameterized activation function that is shown to both improve accuracy and adversarial robustness. The activation functions learned in this work also appear symmetric and have a positive output for a negative input and the effect this shape has on accuracy is investigated. Given this related work, I am not sure what the novel contributions of this work are.

The accuracy on the clean CIFAR-10 images seemed rather low. Typically, Resnet models achieve around 90% accuracy with ReLU [2,3], however, the authors achieve around 83% accuracy with ReLU. Is there a reason for this?

REFERENCES:
[1] Zhao, Qiyang, and Lewis D. Griffin. "Suppressing the unusual: towards robust cnns using symmetric activation functions." arXiv preprint arXiv:1603.05145 (2016).
[2] Tavakoli, Mohammadamin, Forest Agostinelli, and Pierre Baldi. "Splash: Learnable activation functions for improving accuracy and adversarial robustness." Neural Networks 140 (2021): 1-12.
[3] He, Kaiming, et al. "Deep residual learning for image recognition." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2016.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper investigates some potentially interesting directions when it comes to activation functions and adversarial robustness. While the authors find correlation between certain properties of activation functions and adversarial robustness, I do not see evidence for a cause relationship. Related work brings this causal relationship further in to question by offering alternative explanations. Furthermore, the authors do not properly take related work into account. Given the related work, the authors' contributions are unclear.

content.title: Thank you for the feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for the feedback.  Please find our responses below:
> Causal relationship between properties (high curvature, positive outputs on negative inputs) and robustness

It was not our intention to claim a causal relationship between properties in activation shape and robustness.  Rather, Section 3 was intended as a way to guide the design of a new parametric activation function PSSiLU.  However, we agree that the wording may be unclear and we have revised the text to stress the fact that these qualities are correlated, not causal.  Our main contribution is in Section 4, where we then combine all PAFs with adversarial training and demonstrate that even the addition of a few parameters into adversarial training can significantly improve robust performance.  We have updated the text in the abstract, introduction, and Section 3 to make this more clear.

> Related work

As mentioned, the main contribution of our paper is the *combination of PAFs with adversarial training*, which is different from the papers referenced by the reviewer since these papers do not use adversarial training.  However, we can summarize additional differences between Section 3 of our paper and the referenced papers and incorporate a discussion into our paper:
Zhao et al. investigate the impact of using symmetric activation functions on robustness; however, they investigate cases such as RBF where the end behavior of the activation functions tend towards 0.  Their conclusion is that these symmetric activation functions can help suppress adversarial signals.  In our case, all PAFS tend towards either $\infty$ or $-\infty$ on positive inputs, so the same idea of suppressing adversarial signals does not necessarily hold in our case.  The trends observed in Section 3 cannot completely be explained by Zhao et al.
Tavakoli et al. introduce a learnable symmetric piecewise linear PAF called SPLASH and trains this activation function using standard training.  In comparison, we investigate a number of PAFs with nonlinear components such as PELU, PSoftplus, PSiLU, ReBLU, etc.  Our choice in activation function also allows us to investigate the impact of factors such as smoothness when combining with adversarial training.  Additionally, Tavakoli et al. experiment with 7 linear components in SPLASH, which adds a total of 12 additional parameters at each layer in the network architecture.  In our case, the incorporation of parameters is minimal, each activation function introduces 1 (or 2 in the case of PSSiLU) total into the network (since these parameters are shared).  Thus, an additional important result of our paper is that we demonstrate that we can significantly improve robustness through adversarial training without significantly increasing the capacity of the model architecture.  Another difference is that Tavakoli et al. evaluates SPLASH with parameters learned through standard training, so it is unclear whether other configurations of SPLASH parameters can lead to better performance.  In comparison, we manually evaluate a range of fixed parameter values in the standard trained setting (Section 3) and visualize shapes learned in the adversarially trained setting (Section 4).
We have also added a discussion of related works including Tavakoli et al. in Appendix B.

> Accuracy on clean CIFAR-10 images seems low

The accuracies reported in Section 4 are accuracies for adversarially trained models, which are generally lower than 90% for WRN-28-10 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 (as can be seen on RobustBench [Croce et al.]).
Croce, Francesco, et al. "Robustbench: a standardized adversarial robustness benchmark." arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.09670 (2020).

content.title: Thank you for the feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for the feedback.  Please find our responses below:
> Improvement over ReLU is marginal

We respectfully disagree. From Table 1, PSSiLU improves over ReLU by 2.69% while PSoftplus and PSiLU improve over ReLU by 1.67% and 1.10% respectively.  From Table 2, we also see that on ResNet-18 the PSSiLU improves performance by 4.54%.  This gap is quite large when considering that we are essentially adding 1-2 parameters into the network overall.  For context, [1] performs a study on varying the width and depth of WRN on robustness through adversarial training and in Figure 3 of [1], you can see that it takes millions of additional parameters by varying width and depth in order to achieve a 1-2% increase in robustness.  Another example can be seen on RobustBench where [2] uses 100 million DDPM images when training a WRN-28-10 model and a WRN-70-16 model; the WRN-70-16 model achieves 2.72% higher robust accuracy but has significantly more parameters than WRN-28-10.  We will add more context in our discussion of results in Section 4 to make the significance of the improvement more clear.

> PAFs require significantly more data to improve over ReLU, which undermines benefits of using PAFs

This is a misunderstanding. The reviewer is correct that the additional data boosts the performance of parametric activation functions. However, we emphasize that in our work, the additional data is *synthetic*, whose source is DDPM, which is a generative model trained on the original dataset of interest. Thus, there is no cost incurred in gathering/labeling additional data. This is further confirmed by our model appearing in the RobustBench leaderboard under the category of “no extra data”. 

As a secondary point,  we note that in many cases,  PSiLU and PSSiLU are able to outperform ReLU even without additional data (as indicated by purple text in Table 2 and in tables in Appendix C).

content.title: Initial paper modifications
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful feedback.  Overall, we noticed that there was some confusion among reviewers about the contributions of this paper.  To clarify, our contributions are concentrated in Section 4, where we leverage learnable PAFs to improve the performance of adversarial training.  Section 3, in which we conduct a search over activation shapes, is introduced to motivate the design of PSSiLU rather than make conclusions about the relationship between activation function shape and robustness.  We agree that the wording used in the paper is confusing and have thus uploaded a revised paper to make this point more clear (revisions are indicated in red).  Additional changes addressing reviewer concerns have also been made as follows:
- Added discussion on comparison with related works Appendix B (Reviewer 2 and 3)
- Added additional context for significance of experimental results (Reviewer 1)
- Removed TI-500k results due to the withdrawal of the TinyImages dataset (Reviewer 4)
We are currently working on adding additional experiments/results suggested by reviewers and will update the paper to include those results.
